opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the simplest way to put it is that predicting the next base well forces the model to learn whatever structure actually generated the sequence. DNA isn't random. Every genome that exists has passed through billions of years of evolution, so the sequences we observe are the survivors, the ones that encode things that work. If you want to guess the next nucleotide accurately across millions of genomes, you can't just memorize. You have to pick up the rules: where a gene starts, what a codon looks like, which amino acid changes a protein will tolerate, how a promoter sits relative to the coding region, how an operon is organized, how a CRISPR array or a toxin-antitoxin system is laid out.

It's the same intuition as with language models. Next-token prediction on text ends up teaching grammar, facts, even some reasoning, because those are the compressed explanations of why the text looks the way it does. In biology, evolution is the author, and the "grammar" is biochemistry and function.

What surprised us, and I think surprised a lot of people, was how far that goes when you train at the DNA level rather than just on proteins. With a long context window, Evo can see across multiple genes, so it starts to learn relationships between molecules, not just single molecules. That's how we could do things like zero-shot fitness prediction, where the model's likelihood of a mutated sequence correlates with experimental measurements of whether that protein or RNA still works, without ever being trained on those labels. And on the generative side, we could prompt it to design things like CRISPR-Cas systems, where you need a protein and an RNA that have to work together, and some of those designs actually function in the lab.

I'd be careful not to overclaim, though. The model learns the statistics of what evolution has produced. That's a powerful prior, but it doesn't mean it understands mechanism the way a biochemist does, and it's weaker in places where evolution hasn't sampled much or where function depends heavily on context it can't see, like cellular environment or regulation in complex eukaryotic genomes. So I think of it as a kind of evolutionary intuition learned from sequence, and the exciting question now is how far scaling, longer context, and pairing it with experimental feedback can push that toward real design.

r001.rationale: The response says next-base prediction forces EVO to learn sequence rules and the “grammar” of biochemistry and function, including relationships among genes and molecules.

r002.rationale: It describes zero-shot fitness prediction: likelihoods of mutated sequences correlate with whether the protein or RNA still works, without training on those labels, conveying functional effects of variants.

astra-6.text:
I think the surprising thing is how much biology you have to learn to get good at predicting the next base. The alphabet is only four letters, but those letters aren’t independent. A sequence has constraints at many different scales: whether it encodes a functional protein, how that protein is regulated, and how it fits into the rest of the organism.

So next-base prediction is a simple training objective, but solving it well can require learning something much richer. If you’re predicting a base in a coding sequence, it helps to capture the constraints on the protein that sequence encodes. With longer context, you also have the opportunity to learn relationships between different parts of the genome.

That doesn’t mean the model automatically understands biology in a causal sense. The important question is whether what it learns transfers: can it predict the effects of mutations, or generate sequences that actually function when you test them? That’s where you start to distinguish a model that captures statistical patterns from one whose representations are useful for doing biology.

r001.rationale: The response explains that next-base prediction requires learning sequence constraints involving protein function, regulation, and the organism, and that the resulting representations may be useful for biology. This conveys learning molecular logic from the objective.

r002.rationale: The response mentions predicting mutation effects, but does not state that EVO can infer the effects of genetic variants whose significance is unknown.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that next-base prediction is a very simple objective, but solving it well can require learning a lot of biology. A genome isn’t a random string of A’s, C’s, G’s, and T’s. It reflects the constraints of evolution: what makes a protein work, how genes are regulated, and how different components function together.

If you train a model across enough diverse genomes, those constraints become useful for predicting what comes next. We don’t explicitly tell Evo, “This is a gene,” or “This sequence regulates that gene.” The question is whether it can discover useful representations of those things through the prediction task itself.

And the important step is testing that. Predicting sequence well isn’t automatically the same as understanding biology. But if the model can predict the effects of mutations or generate sequences that actually function in an experiment, that’s evidence that it has learned something useful beyond the surface statistics of DNA.

r001.rationale: It explains that next-base prediction can reveal useful representations of biological constraints, including protein function, gene regulation, and how components work together.

r002.rationale: It says the model can predict mutation effects, but does not state that it can assess genetic variants whose significance is unknown.
